definition:
Sin, in the Bible's teaching, is any failure to love, trust, and obey God, in act, word, desire, or omission, and the condition of heart and world from which those failures come. It is first of all personal and Godward: David, who had wronged Bathsheba and killed Uriah, still says, “Against You, You only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4), because every wrong done to a neighbor is also a refusal of the God who made that neighbor. But Scripture also speaks of sin as a power that holds people captive, a bent in human nature that no one escapes, and a disorder that spreads into families, cities, and the creation itself. The fall names the event in Genesis 3 by which sin entered a good world; original sin is the Western church's term for the condition every human being is born into as a result. The church confesses together that all have sinned, that sin brings death and alienation from God, and that no one can free themselves. How Adam's sin reaches his descendants is debated, and the site's page on original sin sets out the traditions in full. The work of Christ that answers sin has its own studies under atonement, justification, and repentance; the spiritual powers behind evil are treated under angels and Satan, and the worship of created things under idolatry.

Scripture has no single word for sin; it uses a cluster, each looking at the same reality from a different side. The commonest Hebrew root is chata’, ‘to miss’ or ‘to fail’; the verb is used of Benjamin's slingers who could hit a hair ‘without missing’ (Judges 20:16), though in most of its hundreds of uses it simply means ‘sin’, and ‘missing the mark’ describes its range rather than a hidden original meaning. The noun chatta’t also names the sin offering. ‘Awon, usually ‘iniquity’, suggests something bent or twisted, and it can mean the wrong, the guilt that follows, and the punishment that comes, all in one word. Pesha‘, ‘transgression’, is rebellion or breach of trust, the word used of a vassal who breaks with his overlord. Leviticus 16:21 gathers all three: the high priest confesses Israel's “iniquities and rebellious acts” and “all their sins”. The Greek New Testament uses hamartia (sin, often in Paul a power that rules), paraptōma (‘trespass’, a false step), parabasis (‘transgression’ of a known command), anomia (‘lawlessness’, 1 John 3:4), adikia (‘unrighteousness’), and opheilēma (‘debt’, as in the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:12). Together they say that sin is failure, twistedness, rebellion, lawlessness, and debt, not one of these alone.
ot:
Genesis 1 and 2 describe a world without sin, and Genesis 3 tells how it came. The serpent does not first tempt the woman with evil but with doubt about God's word and goodness (“Did God really say”, Genesis 3:1) and with the promise “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5), the offer to decide good and evil for oneself. The consequences come at once and in every direction: shame, hiding from God, blame between the man and the woman, pain in childbirth, a struggle for rule between husband and wife, a cursed ground, and exile from the tree of life. Death, which God had warned of (Genesis 2:17), now shadows every life: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). The chapter never uses the word ‘sin’. It first appears when God warns Cain, “sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it” (Genesis 4:7), picturing sin as a predator waiting, and Cain kills his brother anyway. From there the story widens: Lamech's boasting (Genesis 4:23-24), the violence that fills the earth until God sees that “every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time” (Genesis 6:5), and the tower of Babel, built so that “we may make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). After the flood God says the same thing about the human heart (Genesis 8:21), so the flood cleanses the earth but not the heart.

The Law gives sin a precise shape. At Sinai God describes himself as “forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin” while refusing to clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7). Leviticus distinguishes sins committed ‘unintentionally’, for which sacrifices are provided (Leviticus 4:2), from sinning “defiantly”, literally ‘with a high hand’, which no offering covers (Numbers 15:30). Sin defiles the sanctuary as well as the sinner, and the Day of Atonement cleanses both (Leviticus 16). The histories show sin working in a whole people: in the period of the judges “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25), and the books of Kings trace how the sins of rulers and people led to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Solomon's prayer states the principle plainly: “there is no one who does not sin” (1 Kings 8:46).

The Psalms and Wisdom books turn inward. David's confession after Nathan confronts him traces his sin back to his beginning: “I was sinful when my mother conceived me” (Psalm 51:5), and he asks not only for pardon but for “a clean heart” (Psalm 51:10). Psalm 32 describes the misery of hidden sin and the relief of confession, and Psalm 19 asks cleansing from “hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12). Proverbs asks who can say, “I have kept my heart pure” (Proverbs 20:9), and Ecclesiastes answers that “there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (Ecclesiastes 7:20). The prophets add the language of betrayal. Israel is a rebellious child (Isaiah 1:2), an unfaithful wife (Hosea 1 to 3), a people who have “forsaken Me, the fountain of living water” for “broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13). Their sins include not only idolatry but injustice to the poor, bribery, and violence (Amos 2:6-8; Isaiah 1:21-23; Micah 3:1-3). Isaiah's vision of God's holiness makes him cry, “Woe is me, for I am ruined” (Isaiah 6:5), and his confession, “We all like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6), stands beside the Servant on whom the LORD lays “the iniquity of us all”.

The prophets also conclude that the problem is deeper than behavior. “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure” (Jeremiah 17:9), and Israel can no more change than “the leopard his spots” (Jeremiah 13:23). Sin separates: “your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2). So the prophetic hope is not merely for better conduct but for a new heart given by God: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), and a new covenant in which God will forgive iniquity and remember sin no more (Jeremiah 31:34). The Old Testament thus ends with a diagnosis and a promise, a humanity that cannot heal itself and a God who says he will.
nt:
The New Testament opens with a name that answers the problem: “you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21), and John the Baptist points to “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Jesus moves sin from the surface to the heart. Anger is the root of murder and lustful looking is adultery “in his heart” (Matthew 5:22, 28), and it is “from within the hearts of men” that evil thoughts and deeds come (Mark 7:21). He speaks of sin as slavery: “everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). He calls it a debt in the prayer he taught (Matthew 6:12), and in his parables it is the lost son's wasted inheritance and his return: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you” (Luke 15:18). He also warns of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which ‘will never be forgiven’ (Mark 3:29), a warning that in its setting concerns those who called the Spirit's work in Jesus the work of Satan. Above all he eats with sinners and forgives them, to the scandal of the righteous, and the tax collector who prays, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner’, goes home justified (Luke 18:13-14).

Paul gives the fullest account. In Romans 1 humanity knew God but “neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him”, and “exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:21, 25); the disorders of human life follow from that exchange, as God gives people over to what they chose. In Romans 3 Paul strings together psalms and prophets to conclude that “Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin” and that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:9, 23). In Romans 5 he traces it to Adam: “sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12), and “through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners” (Romans 5:19). The last phrase of verse 12, eph’ hō, is rendered ‘because all sinned’ by most modern translations, and was read in the Latin Bible Augustine used as ‘in whom all sinned’; how Adam's sin reaches us turns in part on that phrase and on verses 18 and 19. In Paul's letters hamartia often acts like a ruler: it “reigned in death” (Romans 5:21), pays wages (Romans 6:23), uses even God's good law as an opportunity (Romans 7:8), and dwells in a person, so that “what I want to do, I do not do” (Romans 7:15). Paul calls the unbeliever “dead in your trespasses and sins” and “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:1, 3), and calls the power at work in fallen human life ‘the flesh’ (sarx), which “craves what is contrary to the Spirit” (Galatians 5:17). Sin also reaches the creation, which “was subjected to futility” and groans for freedom (Romans 8:20-22).

The New Testament's answer is as large as its diagnosis. God sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin” and “condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3); “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Believers died with Christ so “that we should no longer be slaves to sin” (Romans 6:6), and they are told, “sin shall not be your master” (Romans 6:14). Yet the struggle continues. James describes how desire conceives and “gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (James 1:15), and adds that knowing the good and not doing it is sin (James 4:17). John holds two things together: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves”, and “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:8-9). He defines sin as lawlessness (1 John 3:4) and distinguishes sin that leads to death from sin that does not (1 John 5:16-17), a distinction interpreters explain in different ways. The Bible's last chapters describe a city where “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3) and where God wipes away every tear, because sin and its fruit, death, are gone.

keyTexts.why: The fall: doubt of God's word, the grasp at being like God, and the shame, blame, curse, and exile that follow. The story every later account of sin looks back to.
The Bible's first use of the word sin pictures it crouching at the door, desiring Cain. Sin as a power to be mastered, and a murder that follows when it is not.
Every inclination of the human heart is evil continually, and God is grieved. Sin reaches the heart and wounds God's heart.
God forgives iniquity, transgression, and sin, yet does not clear the guilty. Three words for sin in God's own self-description.
On the Day of Atonement the high priest confesses Israel's iniquities, rebellions, and sins over the goat that bears them away.
David's confession: sin is against God, reaches back to conception, and needs a new heart, not only pardon.
Iniquities build a barrier between people and God. Sin as separation from the God who is able to save.
The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Sin corrupts even our ability to see our sin.
God promises to cleanse his people and give a new heart and his Spirit. The Old Testament's answer to the heart's disease.
Jesus teaches that defilement comes from within, from the heart. Sin is not a matter of the surface.
Everyone who sins is a slave to sin, and the Son sets free. Sin as bondage and Christ as liberator.
Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin, and no one seeks God. The universal verdict drawn from the Psalms and Prophets.
Sin and death enter through Adam and spread to all; grace and life come through Christ. The center of the debate over original sin.
The struggle of a person who wants the good and does the evil, ending in thanks to God through Christ. Read by some of the believer's struggle and by others of life under the law.
Denying sin is self-deception, and confession meets God's faithfulness and forgiveness. The honest center of the Christian life.

history:
The early church taught that sin entered the world through Adam and that Christ undid it; Irenaeus (Against Heresies, about 180) described Christ as recapitulating human history, succeeding where Adam failed. The decisive debate came in the early fifth century. Pelagius, a British ascetic teaching in Rome, and his follower Caelestius taught that human nature remained able to obey God and that Adam harmed his descendants chiefly by example. Augustine of Hippo argued that the whole race was bound in Adam's fall, inheriting both a disordered love and guilt, and that only grace can free the will. The Council of Carthage (418) condemned Pelagian teaching, the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Caelestius, and the Second Council of Orange (529), a regional synod later widely received in the West, rejected the view that a person can begin to turn to God without grace. The Eastern churches, reading Romans 5:12 in Greek, spoke of ancestral sin, the inheritance of death and corruption, rather than inherited guilt. In the monastic tradition Evagrius Ponticus (died 399) described eight evil thoughts, and Gregory the Great's Morals on Job (completed around 595) reshaped them into the seven capital sins, headed by pride, a list that shaped medieval preaching and Dante's Purgatorio.

Medieval theologians refined Augustine's account. Anselm of Canterbury, in On the Virgin Conception and Original Sin (about 1100), defined original sin as the absence of the original justice humanity was meant to have, and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II, questions 71 to 89) called original sin that absence in its formal aspect and disordered desire, concupiscence, in its material aspect, and distinguished mortal from venial sins. The Reformation sharpened the question. Luther, in his Lectures on Romans (1515 to 1516), described sin as the self turned in on itself, and the Augsburg Confession (1530, Article II) taught that all are born without fear of God, without trust in him, and with concupiscence, and that this is truly sin. The Council of Trent, in its decree on original sin (Session V, 1546), taught that baptism removes the guilt of original sin and that the concupiscence which remains is not sin in the proper sense, though it comes from sin and inclines to it. Reformed confessions, including the Canons of Dort (1619) and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 6), taught that Adam's guilt is imputed to all his descendants and that fallen humanity is wholly corrupted and unable to turn to God. Jacob Arminius and the Remonstrants (1610) affirmed the fall's corruption while teaching that grace preceding faith enables a free response, and John Wesley's The Doctrine of Original Sin (1757) defended human corruption against the optimism of John Taylor of Norwich; Jonathan Edwards published his own treatise on original sin in 1758.

Modern thought pressed new questions. Søren Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety (1844) explored the anxiety that precedes the fall of freedom. Friedrich Schleiermacher (The Christian Faith, 1821 to 1822) and later Walter Rauschenbusch (A Theology for the Social Gospel, 1917) emphasized sin's corporate and social dimensions, and Reinhold Niebuhr's The Nature and Destiny of Man (1941 and 1943) described sin chiefly as pride, the anxious self grasping at security, a theme that made original sin credible to many in the century of the world wars. Valerie Saiving (1960) argued that this account fit men's experience better than women's, for whom the typical temptation might be losing oneself rather than exalting oneself. Liberation theologians spoke of structural sin, and Pope John Paul II's Reconciliatio et Paenitentia (1984) and Sollicitudo Rei Socialis (1987) spoke of social sin and ‘structures of sin’ that grow from personal sins. Recent discussion of human origins has asked how the fall relates to evolutionary history, a question the study of humanity touches.

differ.view: Augustinian and Reformed: corruption and imputed guilt
differ.body: Following Augustine and developed in Reformed theology, this view holds that Adam acted as the head and representative of the human race, so that his guilt is reckoned to all his descendants and his corruption passes to all, reaching every part of the person (total depravity, meaning not that people are as bad as possible but that no faculty is untouched). Its defenders point to Romans 5:18-19, where the many were made sinners through one man's disobedience just as the many are made righteous through one man's obedience; they argue that denying the first imputation weakens the second. Psalm 51:5 and Ephesians 2:3 are read as confirming that sin and wrath are present from the start.

differ.view: Wesleyan and Arminian: corruption met by prevenient grace
differ.body: Arminius and John Wesley affirmed that humanity inherits from Adam a corrupted nature and a will unable to turn to God unaided, and they rejected Pelagianism as firmly as any Reformed theologian. They hold, however, that God gives prevenient grace, grace that goes before, to every person, restoring enough freedom to respond to the gospel, and many in this tradition hold that no one is finally condemned for Adam's sin alone but for refusing the grace given. Its defenders point to John 1:9, Titus 2:11, and the universal scope of Romans 5:18, and to Ezekiel 18:20, where the son does not bear the father's iniquity.

The Orthodox churches speak of ancestral sin. From Adam humanity inherits mortality, corruption, and a nature weakened and inclined to the passions, but not Adam's personal guilt, which they hold belongs only to the one who commits a sin. Its defenders read the Greek of Romans 5:12 as saying that death spread to all ‘because all sinned’, so that death is the inheritance and personal sin follows under its reign, and they cite Ezekiel 18:20. The remedy is pictured first as the healing and raising of a dying humanity, Christ trampling down death by death, rather than first as the cancelling of a legal charge.

differ.view: Roman Catholic: guilt removed, concupiscence remaining
differ.body: Catholic teaching, set out at the Council of Trent (1546) and in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992), holds that original sin is a real state of deprivation of original holiness and justice, transmitted by propagation and not by imitation, and that it is ‘contracted’ rather than ‘committed’. Baptism removes original sin and its guilt entirely, while concupiscence, the inclination to sin, remains as a wound to be fought but is not itself sin. Its defenders argue that this honors both Romans 5 and Paul's statement that there is ‘no condemnation’ for those in Christ (Romans 8:1), while explaining the believer's continuing struggle in Romans 7.

errors:
The church has rejected Pelagianism, the teaching that human nature is essentially sound, that sin spreads only by bad example, and that a person can please God and begin to turn to him without grace. The councils of Carthage (418) and Orange (529) judged that it makes grace an optional help rather than the rescue Scripture describes, and it lives on whenever the Christian life is presented as moral self-improvement. The church has equally rejected the Manichaean idea, which Augustine himself once held, that evil is a substance or that the body and matter are sinful in themselves. Sin is a corruption of good things, not a rival creation; the body is not the problem, and God is not the author of sin (James 1:13).

Other distortions are subtler. One shrinks sin to a list of external rule-breakings, missing Jesus' teaching that it lives in the heart, in pride, contempt, and unbelief (Romans 14:23 says that whatever is not from faith is sin). Another shrinks it to a feeling of guilt or low self-worth to be managed, rather than a real offense against God that needs real forgiveness. A third treats sin as only individual, blind to the injustice built into societies that the prophets condemned, or only social, excusing the individual. Finally, some have taught that believers can reach a state in which they no longer sin at all; 1 John 1:8 stands against it, even as Wesleyan teaching on entire sanctification, which speaks of perfect love rather than sinlessness, is a debate within the church and not this error.
life:
The doctrine of sin is not a gloomy doctrine; it is an honest one, and honesty is where healing begins. It explains why good intentions fail, why the heart deceives itself, and why the same wrongs repeat across generations and nations. It means a Christian need not be shocked by their own failures or by other people's, and need not pretend. Because sin is first against God, confession is spoken to him, and because he is “faithful and just to forgive” (1 John 1:9), confession ends not in despair but in cleansing. It also humbles judgment of others: everyone stands under the same verdict, and the one who sees it most clearly is often the tax collector at the back, praying for mercy.

The doctrine also teaches vigilance without fear. Sin still crouches at the door and still deceives (Hebrews 3:13), so Christians confess to one another, pray for one another, and watch their hearts, not only their actions. Yet sin is no longer master (Romans 6:14). Every act of forgiveness, every broken habit, and every injustice set right is a sign of the day when the curse is lifted and the creation's groaning ends. The honest word about sin is spoken so that the word about grace can be heard.
questions: The Bible uses many words for sin: missing the mark, iniquity, rebellion, trespass, lawlessness, debt. Which of these best describes the sin you notice in yourself, and which one do you tend to overlook?

Jesus located sin in the heart (Mark 7:20-23) and Paul described it as a power that rules (Romans 6 and 7). How does seeing sin as both a choice and a captivity change the way you respond to temptation and to other people's failures?
Where do you see sin not only in individual choices but built into families, institutions, or societies, and how do the prophets' words about injustice help Christians confess and resist it?
